item.title: When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1wx8gg7xw1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all - Published As he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone. Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known. But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path. The drone images seemed clear: no-one had survived. And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him. "I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'" Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies. Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home." Mingma G and Nirmal Purja met in Pakistan in 2021, where they were part of the first team to summit the world's second-highest mountain, K2, during winter. Mingma G knew of Nirmal - or Nims, as he was known - from his Netflix documentary 14 Peaks, in which he successfully climbed the world's 14 highest mountains in just over six months. The pair, both avid climbers from Nepal, had taken different paths. Mingma G came from the Sherpa community and built his reputation as a mountain guide over 20 years. Nims was a former Gurkha and British Special Forces soldier who quickly became one of the world's best-known mountaineers. Many saw Nims as an incredible climber who helped Nepalese climbers gain international recognition in a field dominated by foreigners. But he also had his critics: they said he focused too much on records, and on marketing his expeditions to a growing social media following. In 2024 the New York Times published sexual misconduct allegations from two women, which Purja strongly denied through his lawyer at the time, who said they were "false and defamatory". Purja again denied the allegations in a lengthy interview soon after. Before Mingma G met Nims, he wasn't sure about him: "In the beginning, I had the feeling he was very arrogant." But that changed when their paths crossed five years ago, as competitors on their way to K2, who then decided to climb the mountain together and share the record. Mingma G says he found Nims to be "very kind-hearted, one of the most beautiful human beings I've met". Over the years the two would meet on various mountains around the world: Nims "would always be on Everest". This summer they met again, walking into the Karakoram range, before they would split up for different climbs. Nims headed for Broad Peak and Mingma G for K2, around 8km (five miles) apart. Nims asked Mingma G to wait another day so they could meet once more before embarking on these separate missions, but that meeting never happened. "That was the last thing he told me. I still regret it." On 30 July, "we had perfect weather, sunshine, no winds," Mingma G says. By then, he was leading a team up K2. Nims's team of climbers had joined others to form a larger group of 10 that was making its way up Broad Peak. At 08:30, Mingma G spoke to Kili Pemba Sherpa - better known as Kilu - a childhood friend and expert climber in Nims's group. Snow conditions looked good, Kilu had said, and the two agreed to speak again when they both reached the next camp on their respective mountains. The BBC spoke to two trekkers who spotted the climbers scaling Broad Peak. "We were cheering them on," one says. He took a photo of them on the slope, small silhouettes against the snow. The group continued ascending. But less than an hour later, there was a "thundercrack", the other trekker says: "a huge avalanche, starting from the top going down both sides of Broad Peak". "We were hoping and praying that the climbers were above the avalanche," the first trekker continues. But they couldn't see the silhouettes on the slope. The trekkers' guide notified base camp about what they had witnessed. The cause of the avalanche is still being investigated, but the Alpine Club of Pakistan told the BBC that while it had snowed heavily earlier that week, their initial research suggested that it was caused by the collapse of an ice slab, irrespective of snowfall. By the time Mingma G reached the next camp on K2, his team had not heard from the Broad Peak climbers. They didn't panic because climbers often turn off the radio to save battery life. But something was bothering him. One of the Broad Peak climbers, Wang Zhong, was a close friend and a client. He would normally message Mingma G through his Garmin satellite tracker to let him know he'd arrived safely at the next camp. But there was no message from him. Thousands of metres below, Pakistani mountain guide Waqar Ali says he was also trying to contact the group, but to no avail. He thought they may have been sleeping, in preparation for a final push towards the summit that night. But by 15:00, no-one at base camp had had any contact with the group on Broad Peak. Mingma G was 7,300m up on K2, where communication was difficult. His team started calling officials, families, contacts in Kathmandu and anyone who might have been in touch with the climbers. He says it was probably 20:00 when they first heard that the altitude readings from the Broad Peak climbers' trackers had dramatically fallen: one of them had dropped by around 1,600m. It was too late to climb and too dark to send up a drone, so he decided to wait for sunrise. "I had hope," Mingma G says. Especially for Kilu and Nims, who were "experienced and physically… strong". Early next morning, a drone was sent up and soon after, the operator radioed them. The drone had spotted bodies down the mountain. It looked like there were no survivors. "I was totally blank," Mingma G recalls in a low voice. He wasn't quite ready to accept he had lost so many dear friends at once. "Maybe still I had a feeling they might all be alive [and] wanted somebody to help them get down. That was just something I had in my heart and mind." Later that day, Mingma G called off his K2 expedition. Down at the base of Broad Peak, Waqar wept as he arrived with another climber to start the difficult job of bringing the bodies back. They retrieved the bodies of Nadhira Al Harthy, the first Omani woman to climb Everest, and Pur Bahadur Gurung, a Nepalese climber who had summited 12 of the world's 14 highest peaks. But there were still bodies on the mountain and Mingma G was determined to bring his friends home. When he called Nims's wife and brother-in-law to tell them the tragic news, he says they struggled to believe it. Kilu's wife "couldn't say much, but told me: 'don't leave your brother on the mountain'". Organising the next steps of the recovery mission was complicated. The climbers who'd been heading up K2 with Mingma G were unsettled, he says, and facing pressure from their families to go home. Then there were the logistics. From the drone images, Mingma G thought the bodies could be recovered using a helicopter and a long-line rope, but says he was told this wouldn't be possible. "In Nepal it would have taken like two minutes," he says. The Pakistani army which would have provided the helicopters didn't respond to the BBC's questions. The Alpine Club of Pakistan says a request made on 1 August was approved, but poor weather meant it could not be carried out for days. There was only one other option for Mingma G - a recovery operation on foot. On 1 August, Mingma G says, his team of rescuers set off in search of four bodies they believed they'd seen in the drone shots - those of Nims, Kilu, Zhong and a fellow climber called Nima Sherpa. Gyaljen Sherpa would also be discovered nearby. With the slope so unstable, there was a risk of falling rocks and further avalanches. A larger team could potentially lead to more casualties, but a smaller team would struggle to bring the bodies down. The moment the rescue team reached the bodies and began sending them down on ropes, another avalanche hit, he says. The torrent of snow sent one of the bodies down to the bottom. Three others, including Nims, ended up in a more dangerous position - in the centre of a slope with large pillars of glacial ice precariously balanced to the left and right. If either were to collapse while the rescue team were trying to reach the bodies, the tower of ice could sweep them away. The team needed a new plan. As the days progressed, some of its members started leaving. Their numbers went from nine to six, then four. Given how precarious the slope was, the group decided Mingma G would hang back and monitor by drone, instructing the three climbers. The arduous operation took five to six hours, but they finally managed to bring the bodies back down the slope. The moment Mingma G first saw his friends on the mountain still haunts him. Nims and Kilu had covered their faces with their jackets - Mingma G believes they had seen the deadly avalanche coming and prepared. The two were attached to the same rope, their legs wrapped in it. Mingma G thinks they may have hit each other on the way down - which he fears killed them rather than the fall. "They didn't fall that much, almost 500m. But unfortunately they hit each other a lot, I think. If they were not on the rope, maybe there was a possibility that Nims and Kilu might have survived." The team brought the bodies back down the mountain. They were flown by helicopter to the nearby city of Skardu, then on to the capital Islamabad and finally, home to their families. Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi's body was found a few days later, as was the body of American climber Mallory Geis. The body of Nepalese climber Nawang Thindu Sherpa remains on the mountain. Nims's family say they are deeply grateful to the "extraordinary team led by our brother, Mingma G, who worked in incredibly challenging conditions to bring Nimsdai home". This recovery operation has stayed with Mingma G. It doesn't compare to any other mission he has done. As he looks back with deep sorrow, he feels the end of his career could be coming. Memories of Kilu and Nims - the three of them singing together as they marched up to the summit of a freezing but sunny K2 a few years ago - will always be with him. But, he says, "I'm not sure if it helps, if the memory helps me to keep climbing or it makes me stop." item.title: Firefighters say this antioxidant helped them - their union warns it could be risky
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crk3n5z60pvo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Firefighters say this antioxidant helped them - their union warns it could be risky - Published Days after he helped extinguish the Eaton Fire in Los Angeles, Pasadena Fire Captain David Marquez inhaled his first dose of glutathione on the side of the road outside the Rose Bowl stadium. The wildfire became the second most destructive fire in California's history, killing 19 and destroying 9,000 buildings. "We were having trouble sleeping," he said of his team. "Chronic cough, headache, fatigue - just a really rough set of symptoms following the fire." "I felt much better immediately after the worst exposure of my career," said Marquez, a 25-year veteran of firefighting, who has battled with health issues for years. "We were so desperate because of how messed up we were. We were willing to pretty much try anything," he said. Scientists have long known that inhaling toxic smoke from a fire can cause a huge range of illnesses, including several types of cancers. First responders, like firefighters, are especially susceptible. Firefighters have a 14% increased risk of dying from cancer, external compared to the general American population, according to the US National Institute for Occupational Health and Safety. And as awareness of the risks evolve, so too has interest in alternative - but often unproven and potentially dangerous - treatments. Glutathione, an antioxidant that is naturally produced inside the human body, has been offered as a treatment at some of the largest US wildfires in recent years – including most recently in Spokane, Washington. Anecdotal evidence gathered by clinicians and fire departments has shown promising signs that it could be used to rid firefighters of some of the cancer-causing chemicals they absorb during fires. However, no large-scale research has yet been conducted on its safety and efficacy, and there are concerns over purity and contaminated supplies. The International Association of Fire Fighters (IAFF) issued a rare warning about glutathione last month. It noted two recent recalls due to contaminants at compounding pharmacies that produce glutathione. It also noted scientific trials of other common, naturally-occurring vitamins that were found to increase – rather than decrease – the risk of cancer, although none of those vitamins are used in glutathione treatment. "We don't know if glutathione is effective," said Sean DeCrane, the assistant to the general president for health and safety at the IAFF, which represents over 360,000 firefighters across the US and Canada. "We don't know if it's a placebo effect. We don't know the long-term effect of this type of treatment." DeCrane said his group opposes the way it has been "marketed" to firefighters, including in Spokane where morning briefings fire chiefs to their crews included suggestions that they visit a volunteer tent for treatment. "The lack of research really raised concerns for us," he said. He adds that the IAFF has spoken to "multiple members who said that they did not feel well after the treatment, [and] that they felt worse." "The clinician told them, 'Oh, that's just those metals leaving your body'," he said. The recent rise of glutathione can be traced back to 2017, when a group of naturopaths formed together in Santa Rosa, California, to provide assistance to fire crews combating the Tubbs Fire. The Integrated Health Action Network (IHAN), previously called the Integrative Healers Network, now sends volunteer clinicians to major wildfires across the country to provide glutathione, as well as other naturopathic treatments including acupuncture and massage therapy. In response to the warning from IAFF, the group released a statement agreeing with the need for further testing, and offering to work with researchers to prove glutathione's effectiveness. Co-founder Jen Riegle, who is not a medical doctor but is a licensed naturopath, external, said that glutathione treatment often leads to "clinically-meaningful improvements in headaches, fatigue and brain fog, which are some of the top symptoms we see in firefighters when they're on a fire". The treatments help to force out some of the harmful contaminants in firefighters' bodies, she claims, and can have short-term side effects immediately after treatment. Riegle is hopeful the data the group has collected will spur on further research, and "to prove that this is a good long-term solution for firefighters". But she adds that all of the evidence IHAN has collected is anecdotal, and far from conclusive. "I just want to be really clear that what we are collecting is data that we have because of a treatment programme," she said. "It shouldn't ever be misconstrued as clinical trial data, or double-blind, placebo-controlled, peer-reviewed data. It is just meant as a starting point to be able to garner support for future studies." Medical trials of a new drug typically take years before receiving regulatory approval, and involve rigorous a research and standards. Interest in glutathione rose last year when California's state Board of Pharmacy attempted to pass new rules that would have severely restricted its production. The proposed rule change led to a groundswell of opposition from some firefighters, who travelled to the state capital to testify about how it has improved their health. The plan to further restrict it was later abandoned. Marquez was among the firefighters who went to Sacramento to testify in uniform. He said he is grateful that glutathione is being offered more frequently – including by all fire stations in Pasadena, where he works. He dismisses concerns about its effectiveness, including suggestions that alleviated symptoms could be due to a placebo effect. Using an expletive, Marquez said: "I don't [care] it's a placebo - it was working. Guys were saying they felt better. I felt better. And it made me want to seek out more treatments." Regulations and medicines for firefighters have at times lagged behind the need. Until last year, firefighters for the National Forest Service were banned from wearing face masks due to concerns about their ability to operate in rugged mountain terrains. There is now a growing understanding of the need for respiratory protections and decontamination to help prevent certain cancers that are more common for firefighters. Dr Coralynn Sack, an occupational pulmonologist specialising in air pollution's effects on the body at the University of Washington, said the noxious fumes from wildfires are well known to pose "inhalational hazards" to firefighters. "There's been a lot of interest in using antioxidant supplements for air pollution in general," she said. "Studies have shown mixed responses. Some have even shown worse responses." Sack said there was "biological plausibility" to think such a treatment might work, but said she was "very underwhelmed by the data that exists". There have been no clinical trials on glutathione in firefighters, she added. Sack said the debate over glutathione "shifts the emphasis away from things that we know work" like giving firefighters access to good personal protective equipment. Greg Fonts, a fire captain in West Sacramento and vice-president of his local IAFF chapter, said there is a growing understanding of the importance of firefighter health. Gone are the days of not decontaminating equipment, leaving the ashes on helmets and jackets, in order to boast of past infernos. "When I got the fire service in 2000, I would say that was the attitude was cancer was just part of the job." "Culture has changed drastically," said Fonts, who also has been treated with glutathione. "Younger firefighters are taking health way more seriously."

item.title: Gen Zs recall first learning of 'deeply harrowing, terrifying' 9/11
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgmrzzkjywlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Gen Zs recall first learning of 'deeply harrowing, terrifying' 9/11 - Published Most Americans remember exactly what they were doing and how they felt the day four airplanes were hijacked and crashed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and a field in Pennsylvania. But now, 25 years on from the 11 September 2001 attacks, there is a new generation, too young to remember the day that permanently altered much of American life. Members of Generation Z, born between 1997 and 2012, were told - well after the fact - about the event that undoubtedly reshaped their futures. They carry distinct memories not from the day itself, but from the moment years later that they learned about the attacks. 'Hard to explain what a terrorist is to a child' Avery Black, 20, a journalism student at the University of South Carolina, remembers hearing about 9/11 for the first time in elementary school, then going home and asking her mother about it, she told the BBC. "She just started telling me where she was the day it happened, and just broke down in tears, explaining to me about all the firefighters that went in and never came out," Black recalled. As a child, Black didn't quite grasp the day's gravity, but for her, certain details still stand out. She remembers, most distinctly, the "falling man" – a famous image of a man plummeting, upside down, from the North Tower. A Dallas, Texas native, she also recalls teachers showing the video of then-President George W. Bush first learning about the attacks at an elementary school event. For Annie Erickson, 26, who grew up in North Carolina, personal anecdotes, more than school or reports, created her first memories of 9/11. "My mother grew up in New York City, so I remember my mom telling me about 9/11 and talking about how someone that lived in her building, who she was friends with, passed away in the towers," Erickson said. She also was struck when learning about 9/11 at school that it was one of the few historical events teachers could personalise with their own memories. Currently, there's no national requirement for US schools to teach students about the attacks, and the expectations vary widely by state. Twenty-five states require or expect public schools to teach the events of 9/11, while 13 make 9/11 instruction optional, according to a recent analysis by The Associated Press. But not every state that requires it specifies a curriculum. Allegra Tashjian, 28, who grew up in Wisconsin, said her teacher explained in first or second grade that it was a very important, sombre day and asked if anyone knew why. After a student responded that it was the day planes hit the towers in New York, Tashjian wondered why she had never heard of it before. Later, at home, she recalls asking her mom if she remembered planes crashing in New York. "I remember she kind of paused folding her laundry and was like, 'um no, I don't think I've ever heard anything about that,'" the PhD student said. "For whatever reason at that point, I guess she really didn't want to talk about it." Tashjian, Erickson, Black and several other Gen Zs all told the BBC that they remember hearing a few details about the attacks in school and from their families, but only through their own research did they learn in depth what actually happened that day. Black didn't realise as a child who was behind the attack. "That was the part that I wasn't really taught until I did my own research. It's really hard to explain what a terrorist is to a child." "It really took me until I was like 13 or 14 to sit down and watch news coverage of 9/11, and really process this is a deeply harrowing, terrifying event," said Jack Coyne, 28, a Connecticut native who lives in Boston. Now, as an adult, Coyne said he wishes people had a more nuanced perspective, recognizing 9/11 as a tragedy that also fuelled Islamophobia in the US and led to further deaths in ensuing wars. Professor David Schanzer, who teaches "9/11 & Its Aftermath" at Duke University, wrote this week in a campus magazine commentary that there's still strong interest generations later. His course is full, with dozens on a waitlist. "Ten years ago, I thought student interest was ebbing and I would need to find something else to teach about," he wrote. But current world events, he said, only made young people more curious about what happened 25 years ago on 9/11. "If you want to understand what has gone wrong over the past couple of decades it makes sense to learn about 9/11, the first global catastrophe of the 21st century (the others being the Great Recession and the COVID-19 pandemic)," he wrote. Different generation, different approach Several Gen Zs told the BBC that, despite gaining knowledge about the tragic day, it is still common among peers to actively lighten conversations about 9/11. Thomas Schwartz, a professor of history and political science at Vanderbilt University, said in a recent class discussion, his seniors - born in 2004 or 2005 - remarked on their generation's tendency to "deflect and joke about 9/11". He added that "students from the Northeast, who had parents with personal memories of 9/11, were more careful about this, remarking on the sensitivities in their family about the subject." Erickson said many Gen Zs tend to downplay monumental events or tragedies because either they "can't fully understand their impact" or they're using humour as a coping mechanism "to not have to think too deeply about some of the larger anxieties in our world". Even now as an adult, Tashjian said it's still difficult for her to fathom large numbers of people dying in any event, and she still gravitates toward individual anecdotes to help her understand 9/11's toll. Schanzer contends that learning about 9/11 and understanding its impact remains crucial for younger generations without first-hand knowledge. "But like most significant historical events, one can't fully understand our world today unless you understand why 9/11 occurred and how the United States responded to it," he said.
